name: Leh-Ladakh
tagline: High-desert moonscape of monasteries and turquoise lakes.
whenBlurb: June to September is the only real window, crowned by the Hemis festival in early summer; passes and roads close in winter, so acclimatise carefully for altitude.

ourTake.lede: The single most important thing in Ladakh is to slow down for altitude; give the first two days to acclimatising in Leh before any high pass or lake, because rushing to Pangong on day one is how trips go wrong. Go for the monasteries and the raw high-desert landscape, not a checklist of viewpoints. The season is short, roughly May to September; outside it, most passes and lakes are cut off.
ourTake.comeIf: You want high-desert monasteries, thin blue air and the drama of the Himalaya.
ourTake.skipIf: You have heart or altitude concerns, or want comfort over rawness.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Chamba Camp Thiksey by TUTC
credentials: The Ultimate Travelling Camp (TUTC), the region's defining luxury tented address
Widely covered in Condé Nast Traveller and National Geographic as the icon of Himalayan luxury camping
items.description: The camp that put luxury Ladakh on the map, canvas suites facing the great monastery, run like a grand hotel under the stars.

items.name: Chamba Camp Diskit by TUTC
credentials: The Ultimate Travelling Camp (TUTC), the only luxury tented camp in the Nubra Valley
Sister property to the widely feted Chamba Camp Thiksey
items.description: TUTC's Nubra outpost, safari-style luxury in a high desert valley, apricot orchards and sand dunes at the door.

items.name: Nimmu House
credentials: Featured by Outlook Traveller as a charming heritage hotel in Ladakh
Listed by Secret Retreats, the curated collection of intimate Asian properties
items.description: A restored 1920s noble house at the confluence of the Indus and Zanskar, five heritage rooms and orchard glamping tents, quietly the most characterful stay in Ladakh.

items.name: Stok Palace Heritage Hotel
credentials: 1820 royal residence of the Namgyal dynasty, opened to the public by the Dalai Lama in 1980
Listed by Secret Retreats; part of Heritage Hotels of India
items.description: The summer palace of Ladakh's royal family, opened to a handful of guests, you sleep inside living history, thangkas and antiques included.

items.name: Lchang Nang Retreat, The House of Trees
credentials: One of the few genuine luxury retreats in the Nubra Valley, on the banks of the Nubra River
Recognised in Ladakh luxury-stay coverage for its remote setting and organic-garden dining
items.description: A quiet Nubra retreat on the riverbank, private villas among elm and apricot trees, organic gardens, snow peaks all around.

items.name: Ladakh Sarai
credentials: Established 1978 by British adventure-travel pioneers, Ladakh's pioneering eco resort
Long-standing premier eco property above the Indus, below the Ladakh Range
items.description: Ladakh's original eco resort, yurt-style bungalows in an orchard of willow and apricot, inspired by the old Silk Road caravanserais.

items.name: The Grand Dragon Ladakh
credentials: The region's only certified 5-Star hotel, at 11,562 ft
Third-generation family hotel; L'OCCITANE Hammam Wellness & Spa on site
items.description: Leh's only certified five-star and the town's most reliable fixed-roof address, warm floors, real service, open when the camps are shut.

items.name: Acclimatise in Leh First (The Essential 48 Hours)
items.description: Leh sits at roughly 3,500 metres, and the single most important thing on any Ladakh itinerary is to do almost nothing for the first day or two while your body adjusts. A well-planned trip builds in rest, hydration and an oxygen-aware pace before the high passes and lakes, which is exactly what protects an elder or a child on a multi-generational trip.

items.name: Leh Palace (Lachen Palkar)
items.description: The nine-storey royal palace rises straight out of the old town, built around 1600 by King Sengge Namgyal and modelled, in miniature, on Lhasa's Potala. Climb its dim stairways to the rooftop and the whole Indus Valley and the snow line open up below you.

items.name: Shanti Stupa
items.description: A white-domed Japanese-built peace stupa perched above Changspa at around 4,000 metres, reached by a steep flight of steps or a short drive. Come at sunset, when the town glows amber below and the peaks turn rose, for the loveliest panorama in Leh.

items.name: Namgyal Tsemo Gompa
items.description: The 15th-century hilltop monastery and old fort crowning the ridge above Leh Palace, home to a tall gold-faced Maitreya Buddha and faded murals. The short climb rewards you with the best bird's-eye view over the whole medieval town.

items.name: Leh Old Town
items.description: The warren of mudbrick lanes below the palace, where Central Asian caravan-era houses, tiny mosques and Buddhist shrines lean into each other. A quiet guided walk here, away from the bazaar, is the most human way to feel Leh's Silk Route past.

items.name: The Main Bazaar
items.description: Leh's broad, poplar-lined market street was laid out wide enough for horses, donkeys and camel caravans, and still hums with Ladakhi women selling vegetables, pashmina, apricots and turquoise. It is the town's living room, best browsed slowly in the cool of the evening.

items.name: Hall of Fame Museum
items.description: An Indian Army museum on the road to Kargil, dedicated to the soldiers of the Siachen and Kargil theatres, with weapons, letters and Siachen survival kit on display. It gives sober, moving context to just how contested and high this frontier is.

items.name: Thiksey Monastery (Dawn Prayers & The Maitreya)
items.description: A twelve-storey white-and-ochre monastery cascading down a hill 19 km from Leh, often likened to a small Potala, with a two-storey 15-metre Maitreya Buddha inside. Arrive for the dawn prayer ceremony, when monks blow the long dungchen horns as the sun climbs the Indus Valley, for one of the great mornings of Buddhist Asia.

items.name: Hemis Monastery (The Largest & The Festival)
credentials: Host of the Hemis Festival, Ladakh's largest monastic celebration
items.description: Set in a hidden gorge 45 km from Leh, Hemis is the largest and wealthiest gompa in Ladakh, seat of the Drukpa lineage and keeper of a giant thangka unfurled only once every twelve years. Its June masked-dance festival, honouring Guru Padmasambhava, is the region's most spectacular.

items.name: Diskit Monastery & The Giant Buddha (Nubra)
items.description: The oldest and largest monastery in the Nubra Valley, watched over by a 32-metre statue of the Maitreya Buddha that gazes across the Shyok towards the border. The drive here over Khardung La and the sight of that giant golden Buddha above the desert valley is pure Ladakh.

items.name: Lamayuru Monastery & The Moonland
items.description: One of Ladakh's oldest monasteries, dramatically sited above eroded, cratered yellow hills that everyone calls 'moonland' for their lunar strangeness. Staying overnight to catch its dawn prayers against that surreal terrain is a quieter, older Ladakh than the lakes.

items.name: Alchi Monastery (The Ancient Murals)
items.description: Unusually built on flat ground by the Indus rather than a hilltop, Alchi shelters some of the oldest and finest surviving wall paintings in the Tibetan Buddhist world, dating from the 11th-12th centuries. To stand before these delicate, jewel-bright murals is to see art almost nowhere else has preserved.

items.name: Shey Palace & Monastery
items.description: The former capital of Ladakh, its ruined hilltop palace overlooking one of the largest gold-gilded copper Buddha statues in the region. A short, easy stop from Leh that layers royal history onto the monastery trail.

items.name: Stok Palace & Museum
items.description: The residence of Ladakh's royal family since 1843, part of it now a museum of crowns, thangkas, royal robes and turquoise jewellery. A heritage wing lets a few guests actually stay in the palace, the most regal address in Ladakh.

items.name: Spituk Monastery
items.description: A 15th-century gompa on a hill right beside Leh airport, with a Kali temple opened only during its winter Gustor festival and sweeping views of the Indus. Its closeness to town makes it an easy, atmospheric first monastery while you are still acclimatising.

items.name: Phyang Monastery
items.description: A large, ochre-walled Drikung Kagyu monastery a short drive west of Leh, quieter than the marquee gompas and set among barley terraces. Its July Tsedup festival brings masked cham dances to a place most tour buses skip.

items.name: Likir Monastery
items.description: Known for the enormous gilded open-air Maitreya Buddha that shines above the Sham Valley, plus a small museum of thangkas and old costumes. It anchors the gentle 'baby trek' between villages that makes an ideal acclimatisation walk.

items.name: Matho Monastery (The Oracles)
items.description: The only Sakya-school monastery in Ladakh, famous for its spring Nagrang festival when two monks emerge as blindfolded oracles to foretell the year. A beautifully restored museum here has revived some of Ladakh's finest thangka conservation.

items.name: Basgo Citadel & Maitreya Temples
items.description: The crumbling mud-brick towers of a former royal capital rise above the Indus, sheltering three temples with towering Maitreya statues and rare wall paintings. Listed on the World Monuments watch and gloriously atmospheric, it is one of Ladakh's most overlooked gems.

items.name: Pangong Tso (The Colour-Shifting Lake)
items.description: A 134-km ribbon of high-altitude lake at about 4,350 metres that changes from turquoise to cobalt to grey as the light moves, most of it stretching across the border into Tibet. Reaching its shore across the Chang La is the classic bucket-list image of Ladakh; a private camp lets you have the water at dawn almost to yourself.

items.name: Tso Moriri
items.description: A pristine, less-visited alpine lake at around 4,595 metres in the Changthang wildlife sanctuary, ringed by snow peaks and grazed by the nomadic Changpa and their pashmina goats. Its stillness and bird life reward those willing to go deeper and slower than the Pangong crowds.

items.name: Nubra Valley (Hunder Dunes & Bactrian Camels)
items.description: A wide desert valley where the Shyok and Nubra rivers meet, with pale sand dunes at Hunder and shaggy double-humped Bactrian camels, descendants of the old Silk Route caravans. The sight of camels crossing high-altitude dunes below snow peaks is one of India's most surreal landscapes.

items.name: Khardung La (Among The World's Highest Passes)
credentials: Frequently cited among the world's highest motorable passes (the exact ranking is contested)
items.description: The gateway pass to Nubra, long celebrated as one of the world's highest motorable passes, though its signboard height is disputed and newer BRO passes now sit higher. Standing in the thin air at the prayer-flag-draped top, with the Karakoram unfolding beyond, is a rite of passage every Ladakh traveller wants.

items.name: Chang La
items.description: The high pass on the road to Pangong, another of Ladakh's very high crossings, marked by prayer flags, a tiny tea stall and often snow even in summer. It is the dramatic threshold you cross on the way to the great lakes.

items.name: Umling La (The Highest Motorable Road)
credentials: Widely recognised as the world's highest motorable road, built by the Border Roads Organisation
items.description: A remote Border Roads pass in eastern Ladakh, above 5,800 metres near Demchok, now widely recognised as the highest motorable road in the world. Getting there is a serious, permit-heavy expedition for the truly adventurous, deep in restricted frontier country.

items.name: Magnetic Hill
items.description: A stretch of road on the Leh-Kargil highway where cars in neutral appear to roll uphill, a gravity-defying optical illusion set among stark mountains. A quick, fun stop that always delights younger travellers on the way to the Sangam.

items.name: The Sangam (Indus-Zanskar Confluence)
items.description: The point near Nimmu where the green Zanskar meets the muddier Indus and the two rivers run side by side in distinct colours before merging. It is a striking, easy photo stop, and the launch point for a summer raft on the Zanskar.

items.name: Zanskar River Rafting
items.description: In summer the Zanskar becomes a torrent of blue-green glacial water, offering some of the most scenic white-water rafting in the Himalayas through a deep gorge below Alchi and Chilling. It is the adrenalin counterpoint to the region's quiet monasteries.

items.name: The Chadar Trek (Frozen Zanskar), Context
items.description: In deep winter the Zanskar freezes into a sheet of ice the locals call the 'chadar', once their only winter route to Leh and now a legendary multi-day trek at temperatures near minus thirty. It is a genuine expedition, best understood as a serious, guided winter undertaking rather than a casual add-on.

items.name: Hemis National Park (Snow Leopard Country)
credentials: Home to the highest recorded density of snow leopards of any protected area in the world
items.description: A vast high-altitude park south of Leh with the highest known density of snow leopards of any protected area on earth, plus blue sheep, ibex and Ladakhi urial. A winter tracking expedition here, with expert spotters and warm base camps, is the ultimate wildlife prize for a patient traveller.

items.name: Tso Kar (The White Lake)
items.description: A salt lake on the remote Changthang plateau, its shores crusted white and its marshes alive with black-necked cranes and kiangs (wild asses). Far off the standard circuit, it rewards the birder and the solitude-seeker on the long overland route to Tso Moriri.

items.name: Turtuk Village (Balti Culture)
items.description: A lush Balti village near the Pakistan border, part of India only since 1971 and open to visitors only since 2010, where apricot orchards, Persian-influenced Balti language and warm homestays feel like a different country. It is one of the most fascinating cultural frontiers you can reach in India.

items.name: Hanle & The Dark Sky Reserve
credentials: Within India's first Dark Sky Reserve, and one of the world's highest observatory sites
items.description: Home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory and the heart of India's first Dark Sky Reserve, Hanle sits under some of the clearest, darkest, highest skies on the planet. On a moonless night the Milky Way blazes overhead with a brilliance no city dweller ever sees; village astro-homestays now lend telescopes to guests.

items.name: A Ladakhi Homestay
items.description: Staying in a village home in Sham, Nubra or Rumbak means butter tea, home-grown vegetables and an evening by the stove with a Ladakhi family. It is the most authentic and quietly luxurious counterpoint to a lakeside camp, and it puts money straight into the community.

items.name: The Ultimate Travelling Camp, Chamba Camp Thiksey
items.description: A five-star tented camp below Thiksey monastery, with butler-serviced canvas suites, four-poster beds, fine dining and a spa under the Himalayan sky, open roughly mid-June to late September. It is the benchmark for luxury in Ladakh and can be paired with its sister camp at Diskit in Nubra.

items.name: Nimmu House
items.description: A restored heritage home and luxury tent retreat at Nimmu, 45 minutes from Leh, with organic gardens, Himalayan views and curated treks and yoga in a serene village setting. It is the elegant, intimate alternative to a big camp, and a superb acclimatisation base.

items.name: Ladakhi Thukpa, Momos & Chutagi
items.description: The local table runs on hearty, vegetarian-friendly warmth: thukpa noodle soup, steamed momos, bowtie-pasta chutagi stew, khambir bread and salty butter tea, all suited to the thin cold air. Sampling these in a village kitchen or a good Leh cafe is comfort food with a Central Asian soul.

items.name: Ladakhi Apricots
items.description: The valleys of Nubra and Sham are famous for their sweet apricots, dried on rooftops and pressed into oil, jam and the local raktsey karpo prized variety. In summer, eating them straight from a Turtuk orchard is one of the region's simplest pleasures.

items.name: Mountain Biking Down From Khardung La
items.description: Being driven to the top of Khardung La and freewheeling the long descent back towards Leh is a classic Ladakh adventure, all thin air, hairpins and huge views. With a support vehicle and a good outfitter it is thrilling yet manageable for a fit traveller.

items.name: A Monastery Festival (Cham Masked Dances)
items.description: Across the year the gompas erupt into colour for their festivals, from Hemis and Phyang in summer to Spituk, Stok, Matho and the Dosmoche in winter, when monks in silk brocade and fierce masks perform the cham dances that drive out evil. Timing a visit to one is the single most vivid cultural experience Ladakh offers.

items.name: Sindhu Darshan at Shey
items.description: An early-summer festival on the banks of the Indus at Shey, honouring the river that gives India its name with prayers, music and waters brought from across the country. It is a gentler, riverside celebration that frames the Indus as the spiritual thread of the whole valley.

items.name: Chemrey Monastery
items.description: A photogenic 17th-century gompa cascading down a conical hill on the road towards Pangong, far quieter than Thiksey or Hemis. Its position and its November fire-ceremony festival make it a rewarding detour for those who want monasteries without crowds.

items.name: Stakna Monastery
items.description: A small Drukpa monastery on a hill shaped like a tiger's nose above a bend in the Indus, with lovely valley views and almost no visitors. It is the kind of serene, overlooked gompa that rewards a slow, curious traveller.

items.name: The Sham Valley 'Baby Trek'
items.description: A gentle two-to-three-day village-to-village walk through Likir, Yangthang and Hemis Shukpachan, linking apricot orchards, small monasteries and homestays at modest altitude. It is the ideal soft introduction to Ladakhi trekking for families and first-timers still acclimatising.

items.name: The Confluence Drive to Nubra via Diskit & Hunder
items.description: The full Nubra loop, over Khardung La to Diskit's giant Buddha, the Hunder dunes and camels, then on towards Turtuk, is Ladakh's greatest single road journey. Spread over two or three unhurried, oxygen-aware days it delivers passes, desert, monastery and Balti culture in one arc.

items.name: Chamba Camp Dining by TUTC
credentials: The dining room of TUTC's Chamba Camp, the region's benchmark for luxury table service
items.description: Al-fresco fine dining under Himalayan stars, plated to grand-hotel standard in the middle of the high desert.

items.name: Tsas by Dolkhar
credentials: Among the highest-rated fine-dining tables in Leh on Tripadvisor; the standout of the new Ladakhi dining wave
items.description: Ladakh's most ambitious modern kitchen, regional produce and heritage recipes given a genuine fine-dining hand.

items.name: Bon Appetit
credentials: A perennial fixture near the top of Tripadvisor's Leh restaurant rankings
items.description: A traditional-house setting away from the bazaar, green fields and snow peaks in view, Leh's go-to for a considered meal out.

items.name: The Tibetan Kitchen
credentials: One of Leh's most popular and consistently top-ranked restaurants for regional cuisine on Tripadvisor
items.description: The place to eat momos, thukpa and tingmo done properly, the town's most trusted name for Tibetan and Ladakhi food.

items.name: Gesmo Restaurant
credentials: A long-established Leh institution, one of the oldest continuously running cafés in town
items.description: One of Leh's oldest cafés, decades of feeding travellers fresh bread, cakes and honest plates on the Main Bazaar.

items.name: Chamba Camp Bonfire & Stargazing by TUTC
credentials: The Ultimate Travelling Camp, evening bonfires and high-altitude stargazing, the region's signature after-dark experience
items.description: Ladakh's real nightlife is the sky, a bonfire, a dram and one of the darkest, clearest star fields on Earth.

items.name: Leh café evenings, Gesmo & the Main Bazaar
credentials: Long-established Leh cafés such as Gesmo, the town's genuine evening gathering points
items.description: The town winds down early; a warm café, mint tea and quiet company is as lively as a Leh evening honestly gets.

plan.heading: 6 days in Leh-Ladakh, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Fly into Leh and rest fully at altitude; do nothing more than settle into Nimmu House or The Grand Dragon.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A gentle stroll to Leh Palace and the old town bazaar as your body adjusts.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Light dinner in-house; early night, hydrated.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to Thiksey monastery for the morning prayers and the great Maitreya Buddha.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Continue to Hemis, the largest gompa, and the quiet Stakna above the river.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Leh; dinner at Bon Appétit terrace over the valley.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive west to Alchi, the eleventh-century monastery complex with its rare Kashmiri murals.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Visit Likir and the confluence at Sangam where the Zanskar meets the Indus.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Stay the night at Nimmu House among the apricot orchards.

days.label: Day 4
days.title: Over the Khardung La to Nubra

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Cross the Khardung La to the Nubra valley, descending to Diskit and its hilltop monastery.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The sand dunes at Hunder and the double-humped camels, late in the day.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Overnight in a Nubra camp or the Lchang Nang retreat, under a full sky.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to Pangong Tso over the Shyok route, arriving to the changing blues of the lake.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow afternoon by the shore; no rush, the light does the work.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Overnight in a premium lakeside camp at Spangmik.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive back to Leh via Chang La, stopping at Shey palace and the Sindhu ghat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A last walk through Leh, tea at a rooftop, some Ladakhi turquoise from a trusted dealer.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Farewell dinner at The Grand Dragon before an early flight.

items.name: Leh town / Changspa
items.description: The main hub for acclimatising, with cafes and the palace above; best for the first days and logistics.

items.name: Nubra Valley (Hunder/Diskit)
items.description: Over the Khardung La, with dunes and camel country; suits those going deeper into Ladakh.

items.name: Indus Valley villages (Stok, Shey, Thiksey)
items.description: Quiet monastery villages near Leh; for a serene, scenic base away from town.

events.name: Hemis Festival
events.note: The largest monastic festival in Ladakh, with masked cham dances at Hemis Gompa; dates follow the Tibetan calendar.

events.name: Ladakh Festival
events.note: A week of processions, polo, archery and folk performance across Leh, marking the season's end.

events.name: Losar (Ladakhi New Year)
events.note: The Buddhist new year, an intimate winter festival for those who brave the cold, closed season.

events.name: Sindhu Darshan
events.note: A riverside festival on the banks of the Indus celebrating the river and Ladakhi culture.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Altitude is the real consideration at 3,500m and above: plan a full day of rest in Leh before any excursion, hydrate, and avoid alcohol on arrival; Inner Line Permits are required for Nubra, Pangong and Tso Moriri and are best arranged in advance.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Kushok Bakula Rimpochee airport at Leh, one of the highest commercial airfields in the world, and be met by a private vehicle; take the earliest possible flight, as afternoon winds frequently disrupt the approach.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver with a Ladakh-registered vehicle is essential for the long, high-altitude drives to Nubra, Pangong and the monasteries; within Leh the old town and market are walkable.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Only postpaid Indian SIMs work in Ladakh (prepaid and most eSIMs do not register here), and signal is limited to Leh and a few towns; treat the valleys and lakes as offline.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; carry ample cash, as ATMs are few and cards are accepted only at Leh hotels and larger properties; tipping drivers and guides at trip end is customary.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: June–September is the only sensible window, passes clear, days are bright and dry at altitude. Avoid November–April, when Leh freezes hard and the road passes (Zoji La, Tanglang La) close under snow.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi to Leh (IXL) in about 80 minutes, best flown early morning before the mountain winds pick up, Air India and IndiGo operate it daily; there is no business cabin on the type, so the play is a forward row and a private lounge on the Delhi side. Overland via Srinagar–Leh or Manali–Leh is spectacular but only late May–October.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Leh sits at ~3,500m; altitude is the headline. Plan a full two nights at rest in Leh before any higher excursion (Nubra, Pangong, Khardung La), stay hydrated, and pre-discuss Diamox with a doctor, AMS is common and no respecter of fitness. No special vaccinations. Very safe and low-crime; water only sealed/boiled.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarian and Jain, Ladakhi and the many traveller kitchens run heavily veg (thukpa, momos, dal), and Jain adaptations are understood in Leh's main hotels. Bon Appetit and the better luxury camp/hotel kitchens do clean vegetarian; Indian food is easy to find, though refined Jain fare is best pre-arranged with your property.
